quartiers:Place Carnot and the Halle.name: Place Carnot and the Halle
quartiers:Place Carnot and the Halle.teaser: Two linked squares where Beaune shops, sits and crosses: the café terraces, the market hall, the glazed roof
quartiers:Place Carnot and the Halle.story: Inside a ring of ramparts barely 700 metres across, everything funnels here. Place Carnot is the town's front room: café terraces, the summer brocante, the whole of Beaune crossing on foot between the shops. A few steps south, Place de la Halle holds the covered market hall that fills on Saturday mornings with producers down from the hill villages, and one block on the coloured tiles of the Hôtel-Dieu show over the rooftops. Mulot & Petitjean's spice-bread shop sits at 1 Place Carnot; the Marché aux Vins and its candlelit chapels are a short walk away. Smell it at nine: coffee, warm bread, wet stone.

quartiers:Rue Maufoux and the cellar str.teaser: Négociant doorways above, vaulted cellars below, and a street called Hell that stays cold in July
quartiers:Rue Maufoux and the cellar str.story: This is where Beaune's wine trade lives, and most of it is underground. Along rue Maufoux the doorways are négociant houses, carriage arches and brass plates; beneath the paving run the vaults where bottles and barrels sleep. Near the parvis of the Collégiale you choose between rue Paradis and rue d'Enfer, Hell Street. At dusk on a weekday these lanes empty out, and the vents at street level breathe cellar air at your ankles even in high summer, cold stone and a faint smell of wine. Bissoh's charcoal counter is on rue Maufoux at number 42.

quartiers:Place Madeleine and its faubou.story: East of the centre, away from the Hôtel-Dieu queues, Place Madeleine opens onto the Faubourg Madeleine, a street that runs out of the old ring. By day it is a working neighbourhood with little to see. After seven it turns into the town's wine-bar end: lights in shop windows lined with bottles, shared tables, people who live here eating late. Caves Madeleine is at 8 rue du Faubourg-Madeleine and Le Comptoir des Tontons at number 22, both a few minutes' walk from Place Carnot. Come for dinner, not for sights.

quartiers:Place Monge.story: Place Monge is quieter than Carnot and smells better: of parsley jelly and pastry crust. Le Bistrot Bourguignon (8 rue Monge) and Pâtisserie Fabien Berteau (18 rue Monge) are on the same short stretch.

quartiers:Faubourg Bretonnière.name: Faubourg Bretonnière
quartiers:Faubourg Bretonnière.teaser: Out of the old west gate, past a bastion and terraced houses, to the mill where Beaune grinds its mustard
quartiers:Faubourg Bretonnière.story: Leave the ring by the old Porte Bretonnière on the west side and the town loosens: the Bastion Bretonnière at your back, then a long street of terraced houses running out toward the vines. At number 31 stands Edmond Fallot's moutarderie, the family mustard mill that still grinds on granite stones. Nearby lies the Parc de la Bouzaize, the 1883 English garden with its lake and willows, and beyond the last houses the slope of the premier crus begins. On a still day the street smells faintly sharp, of crushed seed and vinegar, near the mill.

quartiers:The vineyard slope.name: The vineyard slope
quartiers:The vineyard slope.teaser: A few hundred metres past the last street you are standing in Beaune's premier crus
quartiers:The vineyard slope.story: West of the ramparts the town stops and the vines start almost at once: the old guide puts the first premier crus about 200 metres past the last house. Clos des Mouches, Les Grèves and Les Teurons climb the east-facing slope of limestone and marl toward the wooded Montagne de Beaune. At the top an orientation table stands beside a monument, near a statue of Notre-Dame de la Libération, and the view runs down over the rows to the roofs of the town. In late October the leaves have turned yellow and rust, and the picked vines smell of earth and wet leaf.

curiosities:The peasant grape that fathe.name: The peasant grape that fathered the whites
curiosities:The peasant grape that fathe.teaser: Chardonnay's other parent is Gouais Blanc, a grape so despised a duke tried to banish it
curiosities:The peasant grape that fathe.story: In 1999 a UC Davis team led by Carole Meredith, with John Bowers as first author, published DNA fingerprints in Science showing that 16 old northeastern French varieties, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Gamay Noir, Melon and Auxerrois among them, are the offspring of Pinot and Gouais Blanc. Gouais was a field grape of peasants, thought so poor that it is no longer planted in France. Burgundy's dukes had already chosen sides: on 31 July 1395 Philip the Bold ordered Gamay out of his vineyards around Beaune and Dijon, calling it 'a very bad and very disloyal plant'. The banished grape turned out to be Chardonnay's sibling.
curiosities:The peasant grape that fathe.why: Order a Bourgogne Aligoté and remember it shares both parents with the Chardonnay on the same list.
facts: Bourgogne Aligoté, Gamay and Chardonnay on any Beaune wine list: three children of the same two parents

The 1999 paper names the parent as Pinot, without saying which Pinot form; many guides write Pinot Noir. A later Cambridge-Stanford study, reported by Decanter, found Gouais was the mother in nine of 12 varieties tested

curiosities:The Pinot that turned white.name: The Pinot that turned white
curiosities:The Pinot that turned white.teaser: A Nuits-Saint-Georges grower found Pinot Noir vines bearing white grapes, and made a wine of them
curiosities:The Pinot that turned white.story: In the 1930s Henri Gouges, a grower in Nuits-Saint-Georges, noticed Pinot Noir vines carrying pale, white-skinned bunches: a natural colour mutation. He took cuttings, built a nursery from them and in time replanted his premier cru La Perrière with the white selection, which Clive Coates nicknamed 'Pinot Gouges'. The domaine made one or two casks of it in 1947 and did not sell it until the 1950s; Gouges shared cuttings with neighbours, so other village growers farm it too. It is not Pinot Blanc bought from a nursery but a Burgundian vine that changed colour on its own, in a red village.
curiosities:The Pinot that turned white.why: Ask a Beaune wine list for Gouges's white La Perrière: a rare Nuits-Saint-Georges premier cru made from a red grape gone white.

curiosities:The vine named for a child k.name: The vine named for a child king
curiosities:The vine named for a child k.teaser: A Beaune premier cru named for a royal birth a Carmelite nun is said to have foretold
curiosities:The vine named for a child k.story: Inside Beaune Les Grèves, a premier cru of about 32 hectares, lies a parcel of 3.92 hectares called the Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus. It belonged to the Carmelites of Beaune. The story told is that Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement, a Carmelite nun devoted to the Child Jesus, foretold the birth of a son to Anne of Austria, thought unable to bear children; the boy, born in 1638, became Louis XIV, and the vine took the Child's name. What is on record is the sale: in 1791, when Church land was sold off as biens nationaux, Bouchard Père & Fils bought it, and the house still holds it alone.

curiosities:Étienne-Jules Marey.name: Étienne-Jules Marey
curiosities:Étienne-Jules Marey.teaser: The Beaune physiologist who shot birds in flight with a camera shaped like a rifle
curiosities:Étienne-Jules Marey.story: Marey was born in Beaune in 1830 to a wine-merchant family and became a physiologist who wanted to see movement the eye cannot catch. In 1882 he built the fusil photographique, a camera shaped like a rifle that took 12 pictures a second of a bird in flight. In October 1888 he showed the Académie des Sciences images on a strip of sensitised paper, moving at 20 a second. His chronophotographs, a runner or a gull broken into overlapping phases on one plate, still look modern. The town put up a monument to him on Place Marey, and the Musée des Beaux-Arts has long kept his name.

curiosities:Gaspard Monge.name: Gaspard Monge
curiosities:Gaspard Monge.teaser: A Beaune trader's son who drew his town so well the army's engineers recruited him
curiosities:Gaspard Monge.story: Gaspard Monge was born in Beaune in 1746, the son of a local merchant, and schooled by the Oratorians. As a teenager he drew a large plan of the town with instruments he had made himself, and the royal engineering school at Mézières took him on. There he worked out descriptive geometry, the method engineers used to draw solids on flat paper. He was Minister of the Navy for the young Republic in 1792-93, and in 1794 helped found the school that became the École polytechnique, with Lazare Carnot and Lamblardie. Napoleon later made him a count. His bronze stands on the square named for him.
curiosities:Gaspard Monge.why: Find his statue on Place Monge, then walk the few steps to the street where he was born.

culture:The Hôtel-Dieu.name: The Hôtel-Dieu
culture:The Hôtel-Dieu.teaser: A hospital for the poor under a roof of glazed tiles, with its ward of red-curtained beds intact
culture:The Hôtel-Dieu.story: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hôtel-Dieu in 1443 as a free hospital for the poor; it took patients until 1971. From the street it is a grey slate front and a spire. Cross into the courtyard and the roof explodes into glazed tiles laid in patterns of amber, black and green. The Grande Salle des Pôvres runs about 50 metres under a timber vault shaped like an upturned ship's hull, made by the Beaune carpenter Guillaume La Rathe; red-curtained beds line both walls, each once shared by two patients.

culture:The Last Judgment.name: The Last Judgment
culture:The Last Judgment.teaser: Rogier van der Weyden's altarpiece: an archangel weighing souls, the faces readable through a lens
culture:The Last Judgment.story: Rolin commissioned it from Rogier van der Weyden, the leading painter of the Burgundian Netherlands, for the chapel altar of the Salle des Pôvres. It is fifteen paintings on nine panels, six painted on both sides, made around 1443-1451. At the centre, Christ sits on a rainbow; below him the Archangel Michael holds the scales with a soul in each pan, and the saved and the damned part to left and right. Moved in the 20th century to its own room, away from light and crowds, it is read through a magnifying lens.

culture:Collégiale Notre-Dame.name: Collégiale Notre-Dame
culture:Collégiale Notre-Dame.teaser: A Romanesque nave, a small Black Madonna and five tapestries of the Virgin's life, given to the canons in 1500
culture:Collégiale Notre-Dame.story: Built from the 12th century in the Cluniac manner, with Gothic and Renaissance additions, Notre-Dame is one of the last great Romanesque churches of Burgundy. On a weekday morning the long stone nave is often empty, light falling grey and gold on the piers, and in the choir a small 12th-century Black Madonna that is easy to walk past. Behind the choir hang the Tenture de la Vie de la Vierge, five tapestries of the life of the Virgin in wool and silk, handed to the chapter of canons in 1500. Their visiting season ends on 31 October.

Inside are exhibitions on Burgundy's UNESCO-listed vineyard landscape, tastings and wine courses; at the top a panoramic terrace faces the slope of the Côte de Beaune. Go before you walk the vineyards, and the hill you see from the terrace will make sense on foot.

provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.name: Fromagerie Alain Hess
provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.teaser: A Meilleur Ouvrier de France on Place Carnot, and his mustard-seed Délice de Pommard
provisioning:Fromagerie Alain Hess.story: Alain Hess took the Meilleur Ouvrier de France title as a fromager in 1997 and moved his shop onto Place Carnot in 2005. Around 200 cheeses fill the counters, with wine, charcuterie and Italian and Spanish fine food behind. The one to buy is made in-house: the Délice de Pommard, a small triple-crème ball of about 100 g, rolled in mustard seed, named for the village where the first Hess workshop stood. around:The Route des Grands Crus.teaser: France's oldest signposted wine road, 60 km from Dijon to Santenay through the grand cru villages
around:The Route des Grands Crus.story: The Côte-d'Or département created it in 1937, in the wake of France's first paid holidays: a 60-kilometre road from Dijon to Santenay, marked by brown signs with a bunch of grapes, through 37 or 38 villages depending on who counts. Since 4 July 2015 the vineyard landscape it crosses, the Climats, has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

avoid:The frozen-snail menu.teaser: 'Escargots de Bourgogne' near the Hôtel-Dieu are rarely Burgundian: ask where the snails come from
avoid:The frozen-snail menu.story: Around the monuments, set menus open with a dozen 'escargots de Bourgogne' in garlic-and-parsley butter, usually frozen and ready-made. The name is the species, Helix pomatia, not the origin. France has controlled the picking of wild Burgundy snails since a ministerial decree of 24 April 1979, issued because the snail had grown scarce: none may be taken under 3 cm, none at all from 1 April to 30 June, and each département can ban picking outright. Most of what reaches the plate is imported. An honest kitchen will tell you which you are getting.

facts: Ask, before ordering, whether the snails are Helix pomatia and where they come from

avoid:Tasting and driving the Route.story: Driving the Route des Grands Crus from one tasting room to the next is the obvious plan and the wrong one. In France the legal limit is 0.5 g of alcohol per litre of blood; for anyone on a probationary licence, the first three years (two after accompanied driving), it is 0.2 g/l, which one glass can pass. From 0.8 g/l it is a criminal offence. Each glass adds roughly 0.2 to 0.25 g/l. The vines are flat enough to walk or cycle, and the TER stops in the wine villages.

listening:La Vapeur, Dijon.story: For a loud night that Beaune cannot give, go north to Dijon. La Vapeur, on avenue de Stalingrad by the Toison d'Or tram stop, is the city's state-labelled contemporary-music venue (SMAC), with a programme of rap, pop, electronic and stage shows. Late in November 2026 its listings include the drag performer Piche on the 21st and the singer Wallace Cleaver on the 26th, presenting his album 'Marcel'. craft:What is sold as Burgundy-made.story: The shelves around the Hôtel-Dieu and Place Carnot sell jar after jar of 'moutarde de Dijon', and the name promises less than it seems. It is a method, brown seed ground with an acid, and the term is not legally tied to Dijon or to Burgundy. Canada supplies roughly 80 per cent of the seed used in French mustard, and French growers, almost all in Burgundy, cover only around a fifth, which is why the 2022 Canadian drought emptied French supermarket shelves. The jar that promises Burgundian seed carries the protected name 'Moutarde de Bourgogne' IGP. The snail on the souvenir menu is the plate's own warning.

drink:Pinot Noir.story: Every red of the Côte d'Or worth its name is Pinot Noir. The grape stays the same; what changes is the ground. Beaune's own appellation is mostly red, and its premier crus climb the slope just behind the town: Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Champs Pimont. drink:The climat.story: A climat is a named, mapped plot of vines whose wine has been tasted and judged as distinct for centuries: the work of monks, dukes and growers who kept walking the same rows. When UNESCO inscribed the Climats of Burgundy on 4 July 2015, the site took in 1,247 of them along the Côte from Dijon to the Maranges. drink:Kir.story: Félix Kir, canon of the Church, Resistance figure and mayor of Dijon from 1945 to 1968, served white wine and blackcurrant liqueur at every reception, and the drink took his name. The liqueur is Dijon's own: the town's crème de cassis was first made in 1841 by Denis Lagoute, who macerated blackcurrants cold in alcohol. Today Cassis de Dijon is a geographical indication with rules, approved in 2013: made within Dijon, at least 400 g of sugar a litre and 15 percent alcohol, with Noir de Bourgogne or Royal de Naples berries in the mix. One part of it to four or five of sharp Aligoté.

drink:Crémant de Bourgogne.story: Crémant de Bourgogne became an appellation by decree on 17 October 1975, the same day as Crémant de Loire, and the producers marked its fiftieth year in 2025. It is made the way Champagne is: a second fermentation in the bottle, then at least nine months resting on the lees before disgorgement. The longer-aged tiers say so on the label, Éminent at 24 months and Grand Éminent at 36. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead the blend, with Aligoté and Gamay allowed. It is the honest bubble of Burgundy at a fraction of the price, and the base of a Kir Royale.

drink:Marc and Fine de Bourgogne.story: After the harvest, nothing is wasted. Marc de Bourgogne is distilled from what remains in the press, the skins, seeds and stalks, then aged at least two years in wood. Fine de Bourgogne comes from wine still carrying its fine lees, drawn off when the barrels are racked, and needs at least three years in oak: rounder, softer, more like a small Cognac.
